title: Sharing one heterogeneity parameter across a bridged network cost little; the interval method mattered more
question: When two subnetworks of a bridged network have different between-study heterogeneity, does a shared tau give the bridged contrast valid intervals, and do stratified or shrunk alternatives do better at realistic study counts?
design: A bridged contrast summing two subnetworks' pooled effects; heterogeneity ratio 1, 2 or 5 in the bridging or the other subnetwork; 3, 6 or 12 studies each; shared, stratified and shrunk REML heterogeneity with Wald and Hartung-Knapp intervals. 15 cells, 2000 replicates each.
answer: Largely yes for a contrast that sums both subnetworks. With one subnetwork five times as heterogeneous, shared, stratified and shrunk heterogeneity models covered within 0.016 of each other (shared 0.906 to 0.932 and stratified 0.917 to 0.943 across 3 to 12 studies per subnetwork), because a shared tau overstates one part's variance and understates the other's. The undercoverage came from ignoring uncertainty in tau: Hartung-Knapp intervals covered 0.97 to 0.997 at three studies, at about 1.5 times the width.
findings: Registered rule: mixed; shared coverage never below 0.90 in the registered cells, lowest 0.897 elsewhere.
Every Wald interval covered about 0.90 to 0.92 at a 5:1 ratio with three studies per subnetwork.
The shared tau estimate sat between the two true values.
not_answered: A contrast drawing on one subnetwork only would carry the shared tau's error without the offset; frequentist REML without priors; no residual-variance arm or IPD. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Bridged contrast formed as the sum of two subnetworks' pooled effects
